entries.name: Character Creation Guide
entries.text: This guide can be used for Players or Dungeon Masters new to the Dungeons and Devil Fruits System. It should be noted that all steps marked with DM’s Choice are optional and do not need to be followed. Those rules are there to bring the system more in line with the setting and provide players with additional tools for their character.

sections.name: Step 1: Choose a Devil Fruit or Haki (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
Begin your character by selecting either a Devil Fruit or Haki to shape your character’s unique abilities with your DM’s help.
Devil Fruits. These powerful, rare fruits grant incredible abilities, but at the cost of the eater’s ability to swim. If you choose a Devil Fruit, consult Chapter 7 of the Dungeons and Devil Fruits Player’s Handbook, the Dungeons and Devil Expanded Fruits Devil Fruit Encyclopedia, or Chapter 6 of this Handbook. Your DM will guide you, either rolling on a generation table for a randomized choice or allowing you to pick a specific fruit.
Haki. Even if you do not consume a Devil Fruit, you may still increase your prowess with Haki over the course of your adventures. In Chapter 5 of this Handbook, you’ll find options to develop this innate power.
For an extra potential, roll for “Qualities of a King” in the Color of the Supreme King Advancement section to determine if you possess this rare Haki type.

sections.name: Step 2: Determine Devil Fruit Scaling (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
The power of a Devil Fruit can grow and evolve over time, adding new layers of depth and strength to your character’s abilities. However, whether your Devil Fruit scales as you progress is up to the DM’s discretion. DMs can refer to Chapter 6 of this Handbook to decide if they want to use scaling rules for Devil Fruits.
This choice affects how your Devil Fruit abilities unfold through your journey, whether they remain consistent or expand in impact as your character grows.

sections.name: Step 3: Determine Universal Features (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, characters possess remarkable endurance that allow them to face incredible challenges and keep fighting. To reflect this in gameplay, DMs can choose to apply Universal Features from Chapter 1 of this Handbook.
These features provide characters with durability that aligns more closely with the One Piece universe, giving players the sense of pushing their limits just like the iconic characters of the series.

sections.name: Step 4: Determine Special Reactions (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
One Piece combat is fast-paced, dynamic, and full of surprises, where quick reflexes often turn the tide of battle. To capture this spirit, DMs can introduce Special Reactions from Chapter 1 of this Handbook.
These special reactions provide characters with additional ways to respond to threats, creating a more versatile combat experience in line with the series.

sections.name: Step 5: Choose a Race
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, countless unique races inhabit the seas, each with their own distinct traits and abilities. Players can explore these options in Chapter 2: Character Races.
When choosing a race, make sure to also select a subrace if one is available, as it adds another layer of individuality to your character.

sections.name: Step 6: Choose a Class
sections.text: Your class defines your character’s core skills and combat style within the crew. Classes and Subclasses can be found in Chapter 3: Character Classes.

sections.name: Step 7: Determine Ability Scores
sections.text:
Much of what your character does in the game depends on his or her six abilities: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. Each ability has a score, which is a number you record on your character sheet.
The six abilities and their use in the game are described in the Using Ability Scores section. The Ability Score Summary table provides a quick reference for what qualities are measured by each ability, what races increases which abilities, and what classes consider each ability particularly important.
You generate your character’s six ability scores randomly. Roll four 6-sided dice and record the total of the highest three dice on a piece of scratch paper. Do this five more times, so that you have six numbers. If you want to save time or don’t like the idea of randomly determining ability scores, you can use the following scores instead: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8.
Now take your six numbers and write each number beside one of your character’s six abilities to assign scores to Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. Afterward, make any changes to your ability scores as a result of your race choice.
After assigning your ability scores, determine your ability modifiers using the Ability Scores and Modifiers table. To determine an ability modifier without consulting the table, subtract 10 from the ability score and then divide the result by 2 (round down). Write the modifier next to each of your scores.

sections.name: Step 8: Pick a Background
sections.text: Your background provides insight into your character’s past, skills, and motivations, helping to shape who they are beyond their combat abilities. Backgrounds can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook, offering a variety of options, from archaeologist to noble, each with unique skills, proficiencies, and starting equipment.

sections.name: Step 9: Pick Your Crew Role
sections.text:
Every member of a pirate crew plays a vital part in its success, and your crew role will define how you contribute to the ship’s journey. Crew roles can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook. Each role provides unique abilities and proficiencies.
Only one player can occupy each crew role, ensuring that every crewmate brings something distinct to the adventure. Choose a role that aligns with your character’s strengths and aspirations.

sections.name: Step 10: Choose Equipment
sections.text:
Your class and background determine your character’s starting equipment, including weapons, armor, and other adventuring gear. Record this equipment on your character sheet. All such items are detailed in Chapter 5 of the Dungeons and Devil Fruits Player’s Handbook.
Your Strength score limits the amount of gear you can carry. Try not to purchase equipment with a total weight (in pounds) exceeding your Strength score times 15. “Using Ability Scores” has more information on carrying capacity.

sections.name: Step 11: Decribe your Character
sections.text: Once you know the basic game aspects of your character, it’s time to flesh them out as a person. Your character needs a name. Spend a few minutes thinking about what they look like and how they behave in general terms.

sections.name: Step 12: Create a Backstory and Dream
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, every pirate has a story and a dream that fuels their journey. Now it’s time to bring your character to life by crafting their backstory and defining the dream that pushes them forward. Example dreams can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook, but for a more personal touch, creating your own unique dream is encouraged.
Consider what has driven your character to join the crew. Did they experience hardship or adventure that ignited their desire for freedom or power? What do they hope to achieve? A dream could be as grand as finding the One Piece or as personal as reuniting with a lost family. Let this vision guide your character’s choices, as it is the heart of their story and will inspire them as they face the challenges of the open sea.

sections.name: Join your Crew!
sections.text: With your character ready, it’s time to set sail and join your crew on a grand adventure! You’ve crafted a unique individual with their own strengths, dreams, and purpose, and now they’re ready to face the vast unknown. Have fun!

entries.name: Universal Features
entries.text: Universal features give the players of your game main character plot armor. So if you want to push the One Piece vibe, take these.

sections.name: Dream Points
sections.text: A character starts with 1 dream point at 1st Level. Each time the character gains a level, they lose any unspent dream points and gain a new total equal to the character’s level. A player can spend a dream point whenever they make an Attack roll, an ability check, or a saving throw. The player can spend the dream point after the roll is made but before any of its results are applied. Spending the dream point allows the player to roll a d6 and add it to The D20, possibly turning a failure into a success. In addition, whenever a character fails a death saving throw, the player can spend one dream point to turn the failure into a success.

sections.name: I Won’t Abandon My Dreams
sections.text: As you lay bloody and dying at the feet of your enemy, your memories and dreams rush through your mind giving you hope. If at any point you reach 0 hit points and you die, instead roll a d20, on a 12 or higher you stand back up and regain 1 hp. If you died because you reached exhaustion level 6, instead go back to exhaustion level 5.

sections.name: Healing Surge
sections.text:
As an action or bonus action (DM Descretion), a character can healing surge and spend up to half his or her Hit Dice (minimum 1). For each Hit Die spent in this way, the player rolls the die and adds the character’s Constitution modifier. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.
A character who uses a healing surge can’t do so again until he or she finishes a short or long rest.
A character regains all spent Hit Dice at the end of a long rest.

entries.name: Crew Recruitment
entries.text:
The following rules are optional and intended for groups and DMs who wish to incorporate resource management into their campaign.
For smaller ships, a party of 4–5 adventurers can manage operations with assigned officer roles. However, as the ship grows in size or complexity, additional crew becomes necessary. These supplementary NPCs, known as Hirelings, can be recruited from seafaring communities—especially bustling port cities.
A general rule of thumb is one officer per ten hirelings to maintain discipline and structure. These officers may oversee departments, supervise tasks, or serve as apprentices under player characters. Hirelings can be assigned as assistants (e.g., an assistant chef or assistant navigator), or given basic maintenance and labor tasks.

sections.name: Hireling Wages
sections.text:
Hirelings require fair treatment, food, lodging, and pay. Use the “Recruit” stat block (see DM Cabin for statblock) for base hirelings, or higher CR NPCs for officers and specialists.
Standard Hireling: ฿15,000 per week (฿60,000 per month)
Specialist Officer: ฿150,000 per week (฿600,000 per month)

sections.name: Loyalty & Mutiny
sections.text:
Poor treatment can sow the seeds of rebellion. Every instance of mistreatment—underpayment, neglect, or abuse—adds a cumulative +10 to your weekly loyalty roll that affected hirelings or fleet crews may begin planning a mutiny. Proper compensation or acts of goodwill reduce this chance.
Conversely, hirelings and fleet crews treated with respect may form bonds with the crew and adds a cumulative -5 to your weekly loyalty roll. Over time, they may become trusted companions, apprentices, or even receive stat improvements.

sections.name: Loyalty Roll
sections.text: Once per week, the DM will roll a 1d100 on the loyalty role table if you have mistreated any of your crew members.

rows: Loyalty
Happy Crew. Your crew continues to be loyal. Each player gains a Inspiration - Pirate Prestige point.
Dissatisfied Crew. Add +25 to the next loyalty roll.
Mutiny. Roll on the Mutiny Table.
Mutiny Amount
Individual Mutiny. Only the individuals who are wronged on the crew will mutiny.
Small Mutiny. Less than half the crew will mutiny.
Mass Mutiny. More than half the crew will mutiny.
Complete Mutiny. All crew members will mutiny against the players.

sections.name: Fleet Command
sections.text:
As a crew’s notoriety and influence grows, a single ship may no longer suffice. In time, captains may expand their domain by assembling a Fleet.
Rather than tracking every gold coin spent on wages across the fleet, DMs may assume that secondary ships are self-sustaining unless impacted by major events such as plunder, ship damage, or mutiny. Allied ships joining the fleet through alliances may not require wages at all.
Additionally, communication between ships is crucial. Den Den Mushi provide long-distance communication, allowing ships to share intelligence and coordinate attacks.
Flagship. The primary vessel, commanded by the crew’s captain.
Fleet Commanders. Trusted lieutenants (PCs or NPCs) who helm additional ships in the fleet.
Fleet Officers & Crew. Each ship maintains its own officer structure, crew, and operations.

sections.name: Fleet Wages
sections.text: Fleets require upkeep to maintain. Use the table below to determine how much the cost of manetaining your fleet will cost. Do not factor in your own vessel when determining the cost.

rows: Fleet Amount
Weekly Cost (total)
฿10,000,000 + ฿1,000,000 per additional ship

sections.name: Fleet Orders
sections.text: Fleet commanders may embark on side missions or independent expeditions under orders from the captain. When a fleet vessel ventures off alone, the DM rolls on the Fleet Event Table each time it reaches a new island or region. They arrive at said islands every time the Flagship reaches one in their travels.

rows: Event

Grow Influence. The fleet spreads your flag across the island, granting your influence over the territory. The Flagship gains passive income from the region, adding ฿200,000 per week to the players earnings for every island in their territory.
Plunder. The fleet finds enough bellies to pay for the fleets
wages for the week.
Warded Off. The fleet was not able to make their way inland
and disembarks to a new island.
Fleet Tragedy. Roll on the Fleet Tragedy Table.
Tragedy
Minor Damage. The ship withstands insignificant scratches and dents which can easily be patched over the remaining duration of the trip.
Major Damage. The ship withstands serious damage and the hit points of its hull are reduced by 50% of its maximum
Broken Parts. A random component other than the hull of the ship is completely destroyed during the encounter.
Plague. The crew becomes diseased during the encounter.
1d100 percent of the crew dies.
Deadly Poison. The crew is poisoned during the encounter.
Half of the crew dies.
Captured. The ship and crew are captured by enemies
during the encounter.
Launched. The ship and crew are suddenly sprung onto a
nearby sky island and become stranded.
Mysterious Disappearance. The ship and crew drop all
communication during the encounter and the entire crew vanishes for unknown reasons. However, the ship can still be recovered.
Complete Annihilation. The ship is completely destroyed and sinks to the bottom of the ocean along with the crew.
